lead: Space vector modulation (SVPWM) turns the three inverter legs into one rotating voltage vector. The six switches give eight states: six active vectors 60° apart and two zero vectors at the origin. In every switching period SVPWM averages the two nearest active vectors with a zero state to make the wanted vector. It exists because it uses the DC bus better than sine-triangle PWM. You meet it in three-phase motor drives, grid-tied inverters and UPS units.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for the six switch states and Chapter 4.4 for the PWM frame of mind.

blocks.text: A three-phase bridge has six switches. Each leg is either top-on or bottom-on. Write S<sub>a</sub> = 1 when the top switch of phase a is on. The state (S<sub>a</sub>,S<sub>b</sub>,S<sub>c</sub>) has eight values: 000, 100, 110, 010, 011, 001, 101, 111. States 000 and 111 put all three output terminals on the same rail, so the load sees zero voltage; call them zero vectors V<sub>0</sub> and V<sub>7</sub>. The other six are active vectors V<sub>1</sub> to V<sub>6</sub>.

For a balanced star load, state 100 gives phase voltages (2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −V<sub>dc</sub>/3). Here V<sub>dc</sub> is the DC bus voltage. Draw these three voltages as one vector in the αβ plane. Every active vector has length 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, not V<sub>dc</sub>/2. The six active vectors are 60° apart and form a hexagon; the zero vectors sit at the centre. The space between V<sub>1</sub> and V<sub>2</sub> is sector 1, and so on up to sector 6.

A wanted three-phase set becomes one reference vector V<sub>ref</sub> of length V<sub>m</sub> rotating at the output frequency. V<sub>m</sub> is the peak phase voltage you want. In sector 1, V<sub>ref</sub> lies between V<sub>1</sub> and V<sub>2</sub>, as the figure shows. SVPWM does not produce V<sub>ref</sub> instantly. It produces it on average over a switching period T<sub>s</sub>.

sections.h3: Dwell times and the linear limit

blocks.text: Vref Ts = V1 T1 + V2 T2 + V0 T0
blocks.where: Vref is the wanted vector; V1 and V2 are the two active vectors of the sector; V0 is a zero vector; T1, T2 and T0 are their times in one period Ts.

blocks.text: For a reference at angle θ from the start of its sector, use V<sub>1</sub> for T<sub>1</sub>, the next active vector V<sub>2</sub> for T<sub>2</sub>, and a zero vector for T<sub>0</sub>.
T1 = ma Ts sin(60° − θ),  T2 = ma Ts sin θ,  T0 = Ts − T1 − T2
blocks.where: ma = √3 Vm / Vdc is the SVPWM modulation index; Ts is the switching period in seconds; θ is the angle inside the sector, from 0 to 60°; T1, T2 and T0 are times in seconds.

blocks.text: Find the sector by measuring the reference angle α from V<sub>1</sub>. Sector number n = floor(α/60°) + 1. Local angle θ = α − (n−1)×60°. The two active vectors are the ones bounding that sector.

The linear limit is T<sub>1</sub> + T<sub>2</sub> ≤ T<sub>s</sub>. Since T<sub>1</sub> + T<sub>2</sub> = ma Ts cos(30° − θ), the worst point is θ = 30°, where the sum is ma Ts. So ma ≤ 1, which means V<sub>m</sub> ≤ V<sub>dc</sub>/√3. For V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V this is 346.4 V peak phase. Sine-triangle PWM stops at V<sub>dc</sub>/2 = 300 V, so SVPWM gives 15.5% more fundamental before overmodulation.

sections.h3: Seven-segment switching and where it is used

blocks.text: T<sub>0</sub> must not be one frozen block with all switches held. Split it between the two zero states. A common seven-segment order for sector 1 over one T<sub>s</sub> is: V<sub>0</sub> for T<sub>0</sub>/4, V<sub>1</sub> for T<sub>1</sub>/2, V<sub>2</sub> for T<sub>2</sub>/2, V<sub>7</sub> for T<sub>0</sub>/2, V<sub>2</sub> for T<sub>2</sub>/2, V<sub>1</sub> for T<sub>1</sub>/2, V<sub>0</sub> for T<sub>0</sub>/4. In bits: 000 → 100 → 110 → 111 → 110 → 100 → 000. Each change flips only one leg. This lowers switching loss and makes the current ripple symmetric about the centre of the period.

The full name is space vector pulse width modulation, SVPWM. It is a carrier-based PWM in disguise: it matches sine-triangle PWM with a common-mode third-harmonic component added to the references. That common-mode part cancels in line-to-line voltages, so the load gets a larger fundamental from the same bus.

Use it in three-phase motor drives for pumps, fans and electric vehicles, in grid-tied inverters (see Chapter 4.9) and in UPS units. At the same switching frequency it gives a higher usable bus voltage and lower current ripple than plain sine-triangle PWM. Digital implementation is simple: find the sector, compute T1, T2 and T0, then load three compare registers.

figure.caption: Six active vectors V1–V6 form a hexagon around the zero vectors; Vref lies between V1 and V2 in sector 1. The two adjacent active vectors and a zero state are averaged over one switching period.

spec.aria: Six active vectors form a hexagon around two zero vectors at the origin, with a reference vector lying between V1 and V2 in the first sector.

examples.question: A three-phase VSI has Vdc = 600 V, output frequency 50 Hz and switching frequency 6 kHz, so Ts = 166.7 μs. The required fundamental phase-voltage peak is Vm = 300 V. At one instant the reference vector is at θ = 20° inside its sector. Find ma, T1, T2, T0 and the two zero-state times. Check that the reference is inside the linear range.
steps: Linear limit: Vdc/√3 = 600/1.732 = 346.4 V peak. Vm = 300 V < 346.4 V, so the reference is in the linear range.

Split T0 equally between the zero states: 12.3 μs total of V0 and 12.3 μs total of V7. In the seven-segment order V0 is used as 6.1 μs at the start and 6.1 μs at the end; V7 is used as one 12.3 μs block in the middle.
examples.answer: ma = 0.866; T1 = 92.8 μs; T2 = 49.4 μs; T0 = 24.5 μs, split as 12.3 μs of V0 and 12.3 μs of V7, with each V0 quarter equal to 6.1 μs.
examples.check:
import math
Vdc = 600.0
Vm = 300.0
fsw = 6000.0
Ts = 1e6 / fsw
theta = math.radians(20.0)
ma = math.sqrt(3.0) * Vm / Vdc
T1 = ma * Ts * math.sin(math.radians(60.0) - theta)
T2 = ma * Ts * math.sin(theta)
T0 = Ts - T1 - T2
print(round(ma, 3))
print(round(T1, 1))
print(round(T2, 1))
print(round(T0, 1))
print(round(T0 / 2.0, 1))
print(round(T0 / 4.0, 1))

traps: Using Vdc/2 as the length of an active vector; it is 2Vdc/3.
Thinking T0 is 'all switches off' or a single state; T0 must be spent as V0 and V7.
Measuring θ from the α-axis in the T1 and T2 formulas instead of from the start of the sector.
Confusing ma with the sine-triangle modulation index; here ma = √3 Vm/Vdc, and ma = 1 already means Vm = Vdc/√3.
Calling Vdc/2 the linear limit; Vdc/2 belongs to sine-triangle PWM, while SVPWM reaches Vdc/√3.

quiz.q: List the eight switch states of a three-phase VSI and say which are zero vectors.
Why is each active space vector 2Vdc/3 long, while the linear limit for the phase peak is only Vdc/√3?
quiz.a: State 100 gives phase voltages 2Vdc/3, −Vdc/3, −Vdc/3; the vector magnitude is 2Vdc/3. Averaging active and zero vectors over a period can produce a fundamental phase peak up to Vdc/√3. The vector length and the phase peak are different quantities.

quiz.q: A VSI has Vdc = 500 V, Vm = 200 V, Ts = 100 μs and the reference is at θ = 30° inside its sector. Find ma, T1, T2 and T0.
Why does SVPWM split T0 between V0 and V7 instead of using only V0?
quiz.a: Using both zero states lets the sequence change only one leg at a time, for example 000 → 100 → 110 → 111. That reduces switching transitions, distributes loss and makes the waveform symmetric about the period centre.

quiz.q: State the linear limit of SVPWM in terms of Vdc and compare it with sine-triangle PWM.
quiz.a: Phase peak Vdc/√3. It is 15.5% above the Vdc/2 limit of sine-triangle PWM.

quiz.q: A reference lies at α = 135°. Which sector is it in, and what is the local angle θ?

beyond: Not for the exam. SVPWM is the inner modulator in most field-oriented drives for induction and permanent-magnet synchronous machines. Industrial code adds dead time, current sampling and overmodulation to reach the six-step limit. Discontinuous PWM variants clamp one phase for part of the cycle to cut switching loss. Research front ends include model predictive control and multilevel SVPWM. Search for 'space vector PWM sector dwell time overmodulation' and 'discontinuous PWM'.
